newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada sets modest cut in job insurance premiums.
newsitem.headline: Canada sets modest cut in job insurance premiums.

text.p: Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin and Human Resources Minister Pierre Pettigrew on Tuesday announced a modest cut in Employment Insurance (EI) premiums paid by employers and employees.

The 1997 EI premium for employees will be reduced to C$2.90 from C$2.95 for every C$100 of insurable earnings. Employers will pay C$4.06 for every C$100 of employee earnings, down from C$4.13, the ministers said in a joint statement.
The maximum insurable earnings will remain C$39,000 in 1997, the same as this year.

The two ministers also announced a new two-year "New Hires" program, under which all employers who paid less than C$60,000 in EI premiums this year will be exempted from such payments in 1997. Firms with up to 100 full-time employees will be eligible for the benefits of the new program.

"Almost 900,000 firms in Canada will be eligible for premium relief under the New Hires program," Pettigrew said in the statement. "This means almost all eligible firms will pay virtually no employer premiums for new employees hired in 1997, and will benefit from a 25 percent reduction in premiums for new employees the following year."
The maximum benefit for a company is C$10,000 each year.
Martin said the cut in EI premiums, which is in effect a modest corporate tax cut, would not jeopardize his deficit reduction targets. He also suggested that more cuts in the future could be made.

"EI premiums will continue to come down, over time, there is no question about that. Keeping our deficit targets has paid off in reducing interest rates to their lowest levels since the beginning of the 1960s and this will pay off in more jobs for Canadians," Martin said.

He has pledged in his budget and a fall fiscal update to bring Canada's federal government budget deficit down to two percent of gross domestic product in fiscal 1997/98 (April-March) and one percent in 1998/99.
Despite more than a year of aggressive interest rate reductions by the Bank of Canada, the country's unemployment rate has remained stubbornly high. It stood at 10.0 percent in October.
